restart_api_pool.detail: Rolling restart of orders-api workers changed nothing: within 25 seconds the pods re-established 200 connections onto the same 4.2s query and Postgres refused the rest.
restart_api_pool.lesson: Restarting orders-api pods had no effect on a database-side slow query.
restart_api_pool.reusable_lesson: Restarting orders-api pods does not help when Postgres connections are exhausted by a slow query: the new workers immediately re-open 200 connections and hit max_connections again within 25 seconds. Diagnose the query instead.

increase_redis_pool_size.detail: Raising the Redis client pool from 100 to 200 changed nothing measurable: the cache was never the constraint (41/100 acquired). Kept as evidence that the recalled Redis playbook does not apply to orders-api.
increase_redis_pool_size.lesson: A memory-driven action targeting the wrong layer: zero effect, and it consumed 10 minutes of incident time.
increase_redis_pool_size.reusable_lesson: Applying the Redis pool playbook to orders-api was ineffective: the cache pool was at 41/100 while the Postgres pool was at 200/200. Always confirm which pool is saturated before applying a remembered runbook.

add_index.detail: CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY on order_items(customer_id) plus ANALYZE dropped the query from 4.2s to 190ms; connections drained to 61/200 and 5xx fell to 0.3%.
add_index.lesson: Indexing the joined table fixed the slow query and released the pool immediately.
add_index.reusable_lesson: When postgres connections are exhausted by a slow scan, CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY on the scanned column plus ANALYZE releases the pool in minutes - prefer this over restarts or pool resizing.

kill_long_running_queries.detail: Terminating the 4.2s queries freed ~180 connections immediately (fail rate 18.4% -> 4.1%) but throughput stayed poor until the index was added, so it is a mitigation that needs a follow-up.
kill_long_running_queries.lesson: Killing long queries restores capacity but not performance; the slow query keeps coming back.
kill_long_running_queries.reusable_lesson: Terminating long-running queries in postgres-orders is a useful emergency lever for connection saturation, but it must be followed by a query fix (index or plan) or the incident returns.

rollback_recent_deploy.detail: Rolling back v4.9.2 removed the analytics join from the default order search path; query p95 fell to 240ms and the pool recovered to 70/200.
rollback_recent_deploy.lesson: The deploy was genuinely implicated here (40 minutes before onset, query-plan change), so the rollback was the right call.
rollback_recent_deploy.reusable_lesson: For orders-api, a release that enables analytics joins on the order search path is a real cause of slow-query connection saturation; rolling it back restores p95 to ~240ms. Confirm the plan change before rolling back, unlike the payment-api cases where the deploy was a lead rather than the cause.

failover_database.detail: HIGH RISK: failing over postgres-orders would drop 200 in-flight transactions and require a replica that is 9 minutes behind. Refused by the safety gate; the warning is displayed instead of an execution plan.
failover_database.lesson: Database failover during connection saturation converts a degraded service into data-loss risk; never automated.
failover_database.reusable_lesson: Do not fail over postgres-orders to fix connection saturation: the replica is behind and it would drop in-flight transactions. A slow query is not a database outage.
